analysis.one_liner: Bans landlords from hiring software that uses rivals' data to set rents together.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the House Judiciary Committee before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a Sherman Act violation for a landlord with 4 or more rental units to pay a company for software that collects pricing, occupancy, and lease-expiration data from competing landlords and then recommends rents. That describes the business model of real-world rent-setting services used by large landlords. It would let the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general enforce the ban, and let renters sue for triple damages without being forced into pre-dispute arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters in buildings owned by large landlords, who could see rents set by competition rather than by a shared pricing algorithm, and could sue for three times their damages with no arbitration clause standing in the way.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for a rental property owner (anyone leasing 4 or more units) to pay a coordinator for pricing services, treating it as a per se Sherman Act violation [S2].

Defines a coordinator as a service that collects prices, supply, and lease termination dates from two or more landlords, analyzes them, and recommends rents, lease terms, or ideal occupancy levels [S2].

Allows anyone injured to sue in federal court for threefold damages, litigation costs, and attorney fees, and voids pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers at the plaintiff's election [S2].
Gives enforcement to the FTC, the Attorney General, and state attorneys general, and lets the FTC sue for civil penalties on its own [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Landlords who lease 4 or more units, who would lose access to shared rent-setting services, and the software companies whose business is feeding competitors' data into rent recommendations.

drawbacks.text: The per se ban sweeps in any subscription to a pricing service, even where the service recommends rents without pooling live competitor data, so a landlord could face automatic liability for using ordinary market tools [S2].

Easier pleading standards and guaranteed treble damages invite litigation costs that small and midsize landlords may pass through to tenants; the same text that helps renters creates a litigation risk borne partly by them [S2].
The definition of residential dwelling units excludes some housing types, and enforcement ultimately depends on the FTC and courts acting, which the bill alone does not guarantee [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For renters in markets dominated by large landlords using shared pricing software, the expected rent relief is real and the enforcement tools are strong. The tradeoffs are real but limited: the per se standard is blunt, and treble-damages litigation could burden smaller landlords. On balance a well-aimed bill whose cost falls on the concentrated parties profiting from the practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never took it up before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Becca Balint introduced the bill on June 5, 2024 [S1][S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the referral [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large landlords and rent-setting software vendors keep the current model; renters gained nothing.

for.name: Becca Balint
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to House Judiciary.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after its referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 sponsors and cosponsors, including the initial co-introducers listed in the bill text, were House Democrats; no Republicans cosponsored [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Rent-setting software and data analytics providers
industries.note: The bill defines their core service — pooling competitors' pricing, occupancy, and lease-expiration data to recommend rents and occupancy targets — as unlawful coordination. Providers of this service would lose the business model the bill targets.

industries.industry: Large residential landlords (4 or more units)
industries.note: They could no longer subscribe to shared pricing services, and renters could sue them for treble damages. Their interest is charging higher rents; renters' interest is lower rents.
